---
title: "Applications and Case Studies"
---

The preceding chapters built representations. This chapter shows what they are used
for end to end: turning a molecule, a variant, a protein, or a cell into a vector and
using that vector to answer a question someone cares about. The organizing
principle is that **the modality dictates the representation, and the question
dictates the metric**. Every application below is stated as a triple of
(representation, downstream model, evaluation), because an embedding is only
meaningful relative to the task and metric applied to it.

Two habits prevent the most common errors. First, always name a baseline: a learned
embedding competes against fingerprints, substitution matrices, similarity search, or
a simple linear model, and that comparison determines whether the representation
added value [@rogers2010extended]. Second, always separate retrospective from
prospective evaluation: a score computed on data resembling the training
distribution is evidence of fit, not of utility.

| Application | Modality | Embedding method | Primary metric | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Protein variant effects | Protein sequence | ESM-2 zero-shot / supervised head | Spearman, AUROC | [@lin2023evolutionary; @brandes2023genome] |
| Protein variant effects | Protein evolution | Generative evolutionary model (EVE) | AUPRC | [@frazer2021disease] |
| Regulatory variant effects | DNA sequence | DeepSEA / Enformer / genomic LM | AUROC, expression correlation | [@alipanahi2015predicting; @avsec2021effective; @dallatorre2024nucleotide] |
| Property / QSAR–QSPR | Molecule | Chemprop D-MPNN, MolFormer | RMSE, AUROC | [@yang2019analyzing; @ross2022large] |
| Virtual screening | Molecule + target | Graph/learned embeddings + scoring | Hit rate, enrichment factor | [@stokes2020deep] |
| Drug repurposing | Knowledge graph | Hetionet + KG embeddings | AUROC, AUPRC | [@himmelstein2017systematic; @bordes2013translating] |
| Function annotation | Protein sequence | ProtENN, contrastive CLEAN | Accuracy, F-max | [@bileschi2022using; @yu2023enzyme] |
| Antibody design | Protein sequence | Language-model-guided mutation | Binding, expression | [@hie2024efficient] |
| Protein design | Structure | ESM-IF, ProteinMPNN | Recovery, in-silico success | [@hsu2022learning; @dauparas2022robust] |
| Generative protein design | Sequence / structure | ProGen, RFdiffusion | Validity, wet-lab assays | [@madani2023large; @watson2023novo] |
| Patient stratification | scRNA-seq | scVI, scGPT, Geneformer | Clustering, AUROC | [@lopez2018deep; @cui2024scgpt; @theodoris2023transfer] |
| Computational pathology | Image + omics | Vision-language model (CONCH) | AUROC | [@lu2024visual] |

Table 14.1: Application → modality → method → metric map. Metrics are those used in
the cited primary source.

## Variant Effect Prediction

::: {.callout-note}
## Definition

**Variant effect prediction (VEP)** estimates the functional consequence of a
genetic change. A **zero-shot** predictor scores a variant using a pretrained
model without any task-specific training on labeled variants, typically by
comparing the model's likelihood of the mutant sequence to that of the wild type.

:::

### Protein variant effects

The simplest embedding-based VEP is the **masked-marginal** score. Let the protein be
an amino-acid sequence $\mathbf{a}=(a_1,\dots,a_L)$ with
$a_i\in\mathcal{V}_{\mathrm{aa}}$ (the 20 standard residues plus special tokens), and
let $\mathbf{a}_{\setminus i}$ denote the same sequence with position $i$ replaced by
a mask symbol. For a single substitution $v$ that replaces the wild-type residue
$a_i$ by a mutant residue $a_i'$, a masked protein language model with parameters
$\theta$ assigns the score

$$
s_{\mathrm{MM}}(v)=\log p_\theta\!\left(a_i'\mid \mathbf{a}_{\setminus i}\right)
-\log p_\theta\!\left(a_i\mid \mathbf{a}_{\setminus i}\right).
$$ {#eq-ch14-vep-score}

The score is a log-likelihood ratio, and its form is not arbitrary. The model's
conditional is a softmax over residues,
$p_\theta(a\mid\mathbf{a}_{\setminus i})=\exp(z_a)/\sum_{a''}\exp(z_{a''})$ with
logits $z_a$, so the normalizer — which depends on the context but not on which
residue is compared — cancels in the difference and @eq-ch14-vep-score reduces to
$z_{a_i'}-z_{a_i}$, the difference of the two residue logits. Using the ratio
therefore isolates the change attributable to the substitution and is invariant to any
context-dependent additive shift of the logits. Because the model is pretrained on
unlabelled sequences and never trained on labelled variants, @eq-ch14-vep-score is a
**zero-shot** estimate; the masked-marginal construction was introduced for protein
language models [@meier2021language] and was reported to correlate with experimental
fitness without fine-tuning at evolutionary scale [@lin2023evolutionary]. Combining
sequence embeddings with structural context — for example by folding the mutant and
comparing local environments — was reported to improve genome-wide prediction of
disease variant effects and to transfer to proteins with little experimental data
[@brandes2023genome]. A complementary route learns the distribution of natural
sequences with a generative model over an alignment and flags variants that fall in
low-density regions, which performs competitively on clinical benchmarks
[@frazer2021disease]. The two families — likelihood-based and density-based — make
different assumptions and often disagree, so a single score should not be treated as
ground truth.

Because these scores are uncalibrated across proteins, a single numeric threshold
rarely transfers. A variant that ranks in the top percentile for a well-represented
protein may be ordinary for a poorly represented one, so predictions should be
reported as within-protein rankings, or recalibrated on labeled variants from the
target family. This is why supervised fine-tuning on even a small set of measured
variants often beats zero-shot scoring for one specific protein.

### Regulatory variant effects

For non-coding variants the unit of prediction is a regulatory signal such as
chromatin accessibility or expression. Let $\mathbf{u}\in\{A,C,G,T\}^{2m+1}$ be the
reference sequence window of radius $m$ centered on the variant, let $\mathbf{u}'$ be
the same window carrying the alternate allele, and let
$g_\phi:\{A,C,G,T\}^{2m+1}\to\mathbb{R}$ be a model with parameters $\phi$ that
predicts a scalar signal. The regulatory effect score is the predicted change

$$
\Delta s_{\mathrm{reg}}(v)=g_\phi(\mathbf{u}')-g_\phi(\mathbf{u}),
$$ {#eq-ch14-vep-reg}

whose magnitude $|\Delta s_{\mathrm{reg}}|$ measures the effect and whose sign gives
its direction. Deep learning on DNA sequence established that these signals are
predictable from local sequence [@alipanahi2015predicting], and Enformer extended the
receptive field to capture long-range interactions and predict expression
quantitatively [@avsec2021effective]; the same construction @eq-ch14-vep-reg applies to
their predicted tracks. Genomic language models
add pretrained representations that transfer across cell types and species
[@ji2021dnabert; @dallatorre2024nucleotide], and long-context architectures widen
the window available to a single forward pass [@nguyen2023hyenadna]. The recurring
failure mode is that a model predicts a regulatory *signal* accurately while the
causal link to disease remains weak; regulatory VEP therefore demands the
leakage-aware evaluation of Chapter 11.

## Drug Discovery

### Property prediction and virtual screening

Molecular embeddings support quantitative structure–activity and structure–property
relationships (QSAR/QSPR). Let a molecule $m$ be embedded as
$\mathbf{x}=f_\theta(m)\in\mathbb{R}^{d}$, and let
$g_\psi:\mathbb{R}^{d}\to\mathbb{R}$ be a prediction head with parameters $\psi$.
Property regression fits

$$
\min_{\psi}\ \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}
\bigl(g_\psi(\mathbf{x}_i)-y_i\bigr)^{2},
$$ {#eq-ch14-qsar}

where $y_i\in\mathbb{R}$ is the measured property (a binding constant, solubility, or
toxicity). Under the Gaussian-noise model of Appendix A, minimizing @eq-ch14-qsar is
maximum-likelihood estimation, which is why squared error is the default objective for
continuous properties; classification replaces it with cross-entropy. Learned graph
representations studied systematically in Chemprop were reported to match or exceed
fixed fingerprints for property regression [@yang2019analyzing], which themselves
remain strong and inexpensive baselines [@rogers2010extended; @jaeger2018mol2vec].
Transformer language models over SMILES provide transferable chemical representations
that rival supervised models on several benchmarks [@ross2022large]. In virtual
screening these representations rank a library. With $A$ actives among $T$ compounds
and the top $k$ of a ranking retrieved, the **enrichment factor** is

$$
\mathrm{EF}_k=\frac{\bigl(\#\{\text{actives in the top }k\}\bigr)/k}{A/T},
$$ {#eq-ch14-ef}

which equals $1$ for a random ranking and grows with the quality of the ranking; @eq-ch14-ef
says nothing about *which* actives are retrieved, so it should be reported alongside a
ranking metric such as precision–recall area. A now-classic demonstration trained a
graph model on growth inhibition data, screened a large compound library, and surfaced
a molecule with broad-spectrum antibacterial activity verified in the laboratory
[@stokes2020deep].
The embedding is a filter, not a proof: hits require experimental confirmation, and
the model's applicability domain is limited to chemistry resembling its training
data.

Evaluation is where screening claims are most fragile. A model validated on
compounds chemically similar to its training set looks excellent and generalizes
poorly, so splits that hold out whole scaffolds, rather than random compounds, give a
more honest estimate. Prospective validation — synthesizing and testing proposed
molecules — remains the strongest evidence, as in the antibacterial screen above
[@stokes2020deep].

### Drug repurposing

Repurposing reframes the problem as link prediction over a biomedical knowledge
graph. Heterogeneous networks integrate drugs, genes, diseases, and pathways, and
embeddings of that graph score candidate drug–disease edges for prioritization
[@himmelstein2017systematic]. Translational and complex-space knowledge-graph
embeddings supply the scoring functions [@bordes2013translating]; in the translational
(TransE) case each drug $h$ (head), relation $r$, and disease $t$ (tail) is represented
by a vector $\mathbf{e}_h,\mathbf{e}_r,\mathbf{e}_t\in\mathbb{R}^{d}$, and a candidate link is scored by

$$
f_r(h,t)=-\lVert\mathbf{e}_h+\mathbf{e}_r-\mathbf{e}_t\rVert_2,
$$ {#eq-ch14-kg}

so the relation acts as a translation in embedding space and larger scores indicate
more plausible drug–disease edges. Training maximizes @eq-ch14-kg on observed edges while
minimizing it on sampled non-edges, which is exactly why retrospective evaluation is
optimistic: a graph that already contains the test edge lets the model score it by
memorization. Predicted target structures from folding models can add a structural
channel [@jumper2021highly]. As with property prediction, the output is a ranked hypothesis;
the evaluation is retrospective area under the curve, which overstates prospective
utility when the graph leaks future edges.

Repurposing evaluations are almost always retrospective, comparing predicted edges
against known drug–disease pairs. Because biomedical knowledge graphs grow by adding
exactly such pairs, a model that memorizes the graph scores well without discovering
anything new. Prospective or temporal splits, in which the model predicts links added
after a cutoff date, are the appropriate test.

## Annotation Transfer and Homology-Free Function Prediction

Classical annotation relies on sequence similarity, which fails for remote homologs.
Embedding methods instead transfer function from learned representations. Deep
protein language models annotate the protein universe with curated family labels
without relying on alignment search [@bileschi2022using], and contrastive learning
places enzymes in a function-aware space that predicts catalytic activity, including
for uncharacterized proteins [@yu2023enzyme]. Embeddings from masked language models
supply general features that feed these heads [@lin2023evolutionary]. The metric of
record is usually classification accuracy or F-max over gene-ontology or enzyme
labels. The honest caveat is that performance is measured on labels derived from the
same databases that shaped the training distribution, so apparent gains can reflect
memorization of annotation artifacts rather than generalization to genuinely novel
families.

The distinction that matters is between interpolating within a known family and
extrapolating to a new one. Embeddings help most when a novel protein sits close to
characterized proteins in representation space, and help least when it does not;
nearest-neighbor distances in the embedding are therefore a useful uncertainty signal
to report alongside the prediction.

## Antibody Design and Protein Engineering

Embeddings guide protein engineering by proposing mutations and ranking designs.
Language-model-guided mutation was reported to improve antibody affinity, with the
model sampling substitutions in context and wet-lab assays confirming gains
[@hie2024efficient].
Structure-conditioned inverse folding — predicting sequence from a backbone — is the
workhorse for design tasks: ProteinMPNN recovers and designs sequences for a given
scaffold [@dauparas2022robust], and ESM-IF does the same from predicted backbones at
scale [@hsu2022learning]. Generative models extend this from ranking to proposing new
sequences and backbones: autoregressive protein language models generate functional
sequences across families [@madani2023large], and diffusion over structure designs
novel folds and functions [@watson2023novo]. Evaluation spans computational recovery
metrics and, decisively, experimental measures — expression, stability, and binding.
Computational scores are necessary but not sufficient; the field's accepted evidence
is a wet-lab binding curve.

## Clinical and Biomarker Embeddings; Patient Stratification

In single-cell settings, cell embeddings from probabilistic and generative models
support clustering patients and identifying markers. scVI provides a latent space
that corrects batch effects while preserving biological variation [@lopez2018deep],
and pretrained cell models transfer across tissues and cohorts [@theodoris2023transfer;
@cui2024scgpt; @hao2024large]. Multimodal pathology models align images with
molecular or textual context, enabling image-based tasks that correlate with omics
[@lu2024visual]. Two caveats dominate. First, integration quality is
metric-dependent, so "good" embeddings can look good or bad depending on the chosen
score; benchmarking studies show that no single method wins on every metric
[@luecken2022benchmarking]. Second, embeddings learned across cohorts can encode
batch or site effects that masquerade as biology. Any stratification claim therefore
requires evaluation on held-out cohorts with batch-aware metrics.

A further practical point is that cell embeddings are usually evaluated for how
cleanly they separate known cell types, which is easier than the clinical question of
predicting outcome. Strong clustering does not imply prognostic value, and the two
should be measured separately.

Across all these applications the same discipline applies: define the decision the
embedding is meant to support, choose the metric that reflects that decision, and
state plainly what the model cannot see.

## Worked Case Study: Zero-Shot Protein Variant Effect Prediction

This case study is a minimal, reproducible-in-principle pipeline for scoring single
amino-acid variants with a pretrained protein language model. It states its inputs,
model, evaluation, and limitations explicitly.

**Pipeline.**

```text
 inputs : sequences (FASTA) + variant table (pos, wt, mut) + labels
    |
    v
 model  : ESM-2 pretrained checkpoint (HuggingFace)
          masked-marginal scoring, no task-specific training
    |
    v
 scores : delta log-probability (mutant minus wild type) per variant
    |
    v
 eval   : rank variants -> AUROC (binary) / Spearman (continuous fitness)
    |
    v
 caveat : sequence only; scores uncalibrated; homologs excluded from splits
```

**Inputs.** A set of protein sequences in FASTA format, each with a table of
single-residue substitutions given as (position, wild-type residue, mutant residue),
together with a label column. Labels are either binary (benign/pathogenic or
active/inactive) or continuous (an experimental fitness value). In a real study the
labels would come from a curated source; here the procedure is described so it can
be applied to whatever labeled set the reader has.

**Model.** A pretrained ESM-2 checkpoint is loaded without any task-specific
training [@lin2023evolutionary]. Scoring is zero-shot: for each variant the wild-type
residue at that position is masked, the model's log-probability of the mutant and of
the wild-type residue is read, and the score is their difference. Formally, for a
variant $v$ at position $i$ of a sequence $\mathbf{a}$ with wild-type residue $a_i\in
\mathcal{V}_{\mathrm{aa}}$ and mutant residue $a_i'$, the scoring function the case
study ranks is

$$
s(v)=\log p_\theta\!\left(a_i'\mid\mathbf{a}_{\setminus i}\right)
-\log p_\theta\!\left(a_i\mid\mathbf{a}_{\setminus i}\right),
$$ {#eq-ch14-case-score}

where $\mathbf{a}_{\setminus i}$ is the sequence with position $i$ masked and $\theta$
are the frozen ESM-2 parameters. This is exactly the masked-marginal score of
@eq-ch14-vep-score; @eq-ch14-case-score fixes it as the single quantity the pipeline ranks and
evaluates. A larger $s(v)$ means the model finds the mutant residue more plausible
than the wild-type residue in its sequence context.

```python
from transformers import AutoTokenizer, AutoModelForMaskedLM
import torch

tok = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained("facebook/esm2_t33_650M_UR50D")
model = AutoModelForMaskedLM.from_pretrained("facebook/esm2_t33_650M_UR50D").eval()

def masked_marginal(seq, pos, wt, mut):
    enc = tok(seq, return_tensors="pt")
    mask_idx = pos + 1  # +1 for the CLS token
    enc["input_ids"][0, mask_idx] = tok.mask_token_id
    with torch.no_grad():
        logits = model(**enc).logits[0, mask_idx]
    logp = logits.log_softmax(-1)
    return (logp[tok.convert_tokens_to_ids(mut)]
            - logp[tok.convert_tokens_to_ids(wt)]).item()
```

**Evaluation.** Rank all variants by score. Report AUROC if labels are binary and
Spearman correlation if they are continuous, on a **held-out** split. For a uniformly
drawn positive–negative variant pair the two statistics are

$$
\mathrm{AUROC}=P\!\left(s^{+}>s^{-}\right)+\tfrac{1}{2}P\!\left(s^{+}=s^{-}\right),
\qquad
\rho_s=1-\frac{6\sum_{i=1}^{n}d_i^{2}}{n(n^{2}-1)},
$$ {#eq-ch14-metrics}

where $s^{+}$ and $s^{-}$ are the scores of a positive and a negative variant, $n$ is
the number of variants, and $d_i$ is the difference between the two ranks of variant
$i$ (the tie-corrected form is used in practice). Both statistics of @eq-ch14-metrics
depend only on the ordering of the scores, which is why they are unaffected by the
calibration problem noted below. Because
pretraining corpora contain many homologs, the split must be at the level of
sequence identity (cluster-then-split), not at the level of individual variants;
otherwise homologous sequences appear in both the "training" distribution and the
test set and inflate the score. Report results against a baseline such as
substitution-matrix scores and state whether the test proteins share any detectable
homology with those seen during pretraining.

**Interpretation.** A high AUROC means the score *ranks* labeled variants well on
this set. It does not mean the model identifies causal mechanisms, nor that the same
threshold applies to another protein. Report the score distribution, the identity of
the hardest cases, and the overlap between test proteins and pretraining data.

**Limitations.** The workflow uses sequence only, so it cannot see structural
contacts, ligand context, or post-translational modifications. It assumes
independence between positions and ignores epistasis. Zero-shot scores are
uncalibrated across proteins, so a fixed cutoff is not portable. Performance is
weakest for variants in disordered regions and for proteins under-represented in the
pretraining corpus. Finally, any labels drawn from a database that also informed the
pretraining data risk circularity. These limitations are not incidental; they
determine when the ranking should inform a decision and when it should only
prioritize experiments.

Reproducing the pipeline requires pinning the model revision, the tokenizer, and the
label source: small differences in masking convention or in which protein isoform is
used change scores enough to affect conclusions, so the exact checkpoint and scoring
code should be recorded with any result.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Key Takeaways

- Every application is a triple of representation, downstream model, and metric;
  the metric must match the question [@rao2019evaluating].
- Protein variant effects can be scored zero-shot from language-model likelihoods
  [@lin2023evolutionary], from structural context [@brandes2023genome], or from
  generative evolutionary densities [@frazer2021disease], and the methods disagree.
- Drug discovery uses embeddings as filters — property models, screening ranks, and
  repurposing hypotheses — that require experimental or prospective confirmation
  [@stokes2020deep; @himmelstein2017systematic].
- Homology-free function annotation is powerful but is measured against
  database-derived labels, so generalization claims need homology-aware splits
  [@bileschi2022using; @yu2023enzyme].
- Antibody and protein engineering are judged by wet-lab assays, not computational
  scores alone [@hie2024efficient; @dauparas2022robust].
- For clinical embeddings, integration quality is metric-dependent and batch
  leakage can masquerade as biology [@luecken2022benchmarking].
:::
